Indonesia,[a] officially the Republic of Indonesia,[b] is a country in Southeast Asia and Oceania, between the Indian and Pacific oceans. Comprising between 13,000 and 17,000 islands—including Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, and parts of Borneo and New Guinea—it is the world's largest archipelagic state and the 14th-largest country by area. Indonesia has extensive tropical forests and marine ecosystems that support some of the world's highest levels of biodiversity.

The Indonesian archipelago has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with evidence of early human presence including fossils of Homo erectus and Homo sapiens, and megalithic sites. By the first millennium BCE, it had become connected to regional and international maritime trade networks. Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms developed by the early centuries CE, followed by the spread of Islam and the growth of Islamic states from the late medieval period. European powers later competed to monopolise trade in the Spice Islands of Maluku during the Age of Discovery. Dutch commercial and colonial control expanded from the 17th century and extended over most of the archipelago by the early 20th century, before Indonesia proclaimed its independence in the aftermath of World War II.

Since independence, Indonesia has experienced separatist conflicts, corruption, political upheaval and natural disasters, alongside democratisation and rapid economic growth. The country today is a presidential republic with an elected legislature and consists of 38 provinces, some of which enjoy greater autonomy than others. Home to over 290 million people, Indonesia ranks fourth in the world by population and has the largest Muslim population of any country. More than half of Indonesians live on Java, the most heavily populated island in the world, while the capital Jakarta is the world's most populous city.

Indonesia has hundreds of ethnic groups and more than 700 languages, as well as diverse regional cultures. This diversity is reflected in the national motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, meaning "unity in diversity". Indonesian, a standardised variety of Malay, is the official and national language and serves as the country's lingua franca. Indonesia has the largest economy in Southeast Asia, with services and industry accounting for most output and economic activity concentrated on Java. Sea and air transport are the primary means of connecting the country's many islands. Indonesia is a middle power active in regional and global affairs and is a member of the United Nations, G20, the Non-Aligned Movement, ASEAN, and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

Etymology

Main article: Names of Indonesia

The name Indonesia is usually explained as a combination of India and the Greek word nesos, together meaning 'Indian islands'.[14] In 1850, George Windsor Earl, an English ethnologist, proposed the terms Indunesians and Malayunesians for the inhabitants of the "Indian Archipelago or Malay Archipelago", preferring the latter because he considered Indunesians too general.[15][16] In the same journal, James Richardson Logan adopted Indonesia as a geographical term for the Indian Archipelago.[17][18]

German ethnographer Adolf Bastian from the University of Berlin gave the term greater scholarly currency by using it in the title of his five-volume work Indonesia, or the Islands of the Malay Archipelago (German: Indonesien oder die Inseln des Malayischen Archipel), published between 1884 and 1894.[19] Dutch scholars nevertheless tended to use Malay Archipelago (Dutch: Maleische Archipel) or the Netherlands East Indies (Nederlandsch Oost Indië). Popular alternatives included Dutch East Indies, Indië, de Oost ("the East"), and, less often, Insulinde.[20]

After 1900, Indonesia became increasingly common in academic and public usage, and Indonesian nationalist organisations adopted it as an expression of national unity and freedom from colonial rule.[14] Among its early Indonesian promoters was Soewardi Soerjaningrat (Ki Hajar Dewantara), who established the Indonesisch Persbureau in The Hague in November 1918, a press bureau that used Indonesia in its name.[21]

History

Main article: History of Indonesia

Prehistory, early states, and Islamisation

Main articles: Prehistoric Indonesia and Spread of Islam in Indonesia

The island of Java has yielded numerous hominin fossils generally attributed to Homo erectus, including the type specimen discovered by Eugène Dubois at Trinil.[23][24] Stone artefacts on Flores show that hominins had reached the island by at least 1.02 million years ago.[25] Homo sapiens had dispersed into Southeast Asia by at least 50,000 years ago.[26] In Sulawesi, narrative cave art has been dated to a minimum age of 51,200 years.[22][27] Flores also yielded remains of the small-bodied hominin Homo floresiensis.[28] Megalithic traditions later developed at different times across the archipelago, and stone monuments were used for burials and to honour or commemorate ancestors.[29]

Beginning in the third millennium BCE, Austronesian-speaking communities moved south from Taiwan through the Philippines and into the Indonesian archipelago, where related languages spread across most of the islands.[30][31] Settlement and subsistence practices varied across the islands, with communities combining fishing, hunting, gathering and cultivation.[32] From around 500 BCE, regional trading networks increasingly connected the archipelago with South and East Asia.[33] Goods, knowledge and technologies circulated through these networks, and, during the early centuries CE, some coastal communities in Borneo, Sumatra, and Java developed into trading ports.[34][35] Indian merchants and religious specialists brought Sanskrit literacy, Hindu and Buddhist practices, and models of kingship that local rulers adopted.[36][37]

Srivijaya, founded in southeastern Sumatra in the late 7th century, grew as a maritime trading polity and a centre of Buddhist learning and religious networks.[38][39] In central Java, rulers supported the construction of major Hindu and Buddhist monuments between the 8th and 10th centuries, including Borobudur and Prambanan.[40] Majapahit emerged in eastern Java in the late 13th century after Raden Wijaya used a Mongol expedition to defeat his rivals and then forced the Mongols to withdraw.[41] Its rulers claimed suzerainty over a wide network of ports across the archipelago, although beyond Java this authority was often exercised indirectly through tributary, ritual, and commercial relationships rather than continuous territorial control.[42]

By the late 13th century, Muslim rule had been established in northern Sumatra. Marco Polo reported that Perlak was a Muslim town during his visit in 1292, and a royal tomb at Pasai dated 1297 records a Muslim ruler there.[43][44] Samudra Pasai became an important pepper port and a major centre for Islamic learning.[45] Islam spread further through maritime trading networks, with Muslim communities becoming established at ports along Java's north coast and elsewhere in the archipelago.[46][47] Majapahit declined during the 15th century, and Demak emerged as an independent north-coast sultanate and an important centre of Javanese Islam.[48] Early conversions were associated with the Wali Sanga, the nine saints traditionally credited with the spread of Islam in Java.[49] Islamic practice there also incorporated elements of older Javanese culture.[50]

European contact and colonial rule

Main articles: Dutch East India Company in Indonesia and Dutch East Indies

Before European arrival, spices from Maluku were already traded through Asian maritime networks in which Javanese and other regional merchants participated.[51][52] In this region, the sultanates of Ternate and Tidore emerged as regional powers during the 15th century.[53] The Portuguese captured Malacca in 1511 and reached Maluku the following year, where they sought control of the spice trade.[54] Dutch expeditions followed in the 1590s, and in 1602 competing Dutch companies were merged into the Dutch East India Company (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, VOC). Its charter authorised it to wage war, build fortresses, and conclude treaties in Asia.[55]

In the 17th century, local states continued to expand, including the Mataram Sultanate across much of Java and the Gowa Sultanate on the southern peninsula of Sulawesi, where the port of Makassar became a major trading centre.[56] In 1619, the VOC captured Jayakarta (present-day Jakarta) and renamed it Batavia. It developed as an administrative and commercial centre and attracted Chinese migrants and others from the archipelago.[57][58] Over the next two centuries, the VOC imposed monopolies to control the spice trade and expanded its influence in Java through military campaigns and intervention in local disputes.[59][60] The VOC was dissolved in 1800 after going bankrupt, and its possessions passed to the Dutch government.[61][62] During the Napoleonic Wars, British forces captured Java in 1811, but was returned to the Dutch in 1816.[63]

In the 19th century, Dutch power expanded across the archipelago and met sustained resistance in Java, Sumatra, and Aceh.[64] The Dutch established an outpost in western New Guinea in 1828 but abandoned it in 1836 and began permanent occupation only after 1898.[65] In Bali, a series of Dutch campaigns since 1846 against the independent kingdoms there culminated in 1908.[66] By the early 20th century, military campaigns and boundary agreements had established Dutch control over a territory that largely corresponded to present-day Indonesia, known then as the Netherlands Indies.[67] The colonial administration ruled several territories directly and governed others through local states whose rulers retained limited authority under Dutch supremacy.[67]

In Java, the Dutch had introduced the Cultivation System in 1830, requiring villagers to devote part of their land and labour to government-designated crops as payment for land tax.[68] Criticism of the system helped establish colonial policy as a subject of public debate in the Netherlands.[69] In 1901, the Dutch government adopted the Ethical Policy, which aimed to improve welfare in the Indies. The policy expanded vernacular schooling, irrigation, and other public services.[68][70] Western-style schooling also expanded, but it reached only a small minority of the population.[71] In 1905, the colonial government also began resettling people from Java to less densely populated islands.[72]

Emergence of Indonesia and independence

Main articles: Indonesian National Awakening and Indonesian National Revolution

Colonial education, despite its limited reach, helped produce an educated elite who became active in the emerging nationalist movements.[73] Several political organisations were founded during this period, including Budi Utomo and Sarekat Islam,[74] followed by the Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI) and the Indonesian National Party.[75] During the 1920s, a shared national identity began to develop through youth associations and a growing body of literature in Malay, which had long been a lingua franca that did not favour any single ethnic group. Intellectuals increasingly called the language Bahasa Indonesia and made it a common medium for the emerging nation.[76] The Youth Pledge in 1928 recognised it as the "language of unity", alongside the ideals of one homeland and one nation, Indonesia.[77][78]

The Great Depression reached the colony in the early 1930s, bringing severe economic hardship and increasing fears among colonial authorities that discontent could strengthen radical nationalist movements. Restrictions on nationalist activity became stricter, and by the mid-1930s, Sukarno, Mohammad Hatta, Sutan Sjahrir, and other non-cooperative nationalist leaders had either been imprisoned or exiled.[79] In 1942, Dutch colonial rule collapsed following the Japanese conquest of the colony during the Pacific War.[80][81]

Japanese occupation imposed martial law, banned political parties and mobilised Indonesians through Japanese-sponsored civil and quasi-military organisations.[82] Wartime shortages and forced labour caused widespread hardship, but the ban on the Dutch language strengthened the public use of the Indonesian language.[83][84] Japanese-sponsored forces such as PETA and the Sumatran Giyugun trained tens of thousands of Indonesians.[85] One day after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, Japanese authorities permitted Indonesian leaders to begin preparing institutions and a constitution for an independent state planned for September 1945.[86]

However, Japan surrendered to the Allies on 15 August 1945. Two days later, Sukarno proclaimed Indonesian independence, with Hatta co-signing the declaration.[87][88] They were named president and vice-president on 18 August.[89] Dutch attempts to restore colonial rule led to a four-year military and diplomatic struggle.[90] International opposition to the Netherlands intensified after its offensive of December 1948, and the United States subsequently pressed the Dutch into negotiations recommended by the United Nations.[91] On 27 December 1949, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty to the federal United States of Indonesia, except over western New Guinea.[92][93] The federal states soon dissolved, and a unitary republic was proclaimed on 17 August 1950.[93]

Sukarno era and Suharto's New Order

Main articles: Liberal democracy period in Indonesia, Guided Democracy in Indonesia, and New Order (Indonesia)
Sukarno (left) and Suharto (right), Indonesia's first two presidents

Indonesia adopted a parliamentary system of government under the 1950 provisional constitution.[94] The early republic faced armed opposition from the Darul Islam rebellion, whose supporters aimed to establish an Islamic state.[95] In February 1958, dissidents in West Sumatra proclaimed its own government before being joined by rebels in Sulawesi. They were seeking reforms to the republic rather than separation but were defeated by the central government.[96] After the Constituent Assembly failed to secure the required majority for a permanent constitution, Sukarno dissolved it by decree in 1959 and restored the 1945 Constitution.[97]

This established Guided Democracy, a system characterised by dominant presidential authority, less regional autonomy and a reduced role for political parties.[98] Under this system, Sukarno expanded the military's political role while supporting the growing PKI as a counterweight.[94] He also promoted state enterprises and import substitution, even as foreign investment declined, inflation soared and shortages of consumer goods worsened by the mid-1960s.[99] The western New Guinea dispute culminated in the US-mediated New York Agreement in 1962, and Indonesia administered the territory in 1963.[100][101] Not long after, Sukarno pursued Konfrontasi, opposing the formation of Malaysia through diplomatic pressure and armed incursions into its territory.[102][103]

After the 30 September Movement killed six generals in 1965, forces of Major General Suharto took control of Jakarta, and the military presented the movement as an attempted coup d'etat by the PKI.[104][105] The ensuing anti-communist campaign spread across the country, with army units working alongside or directing civilian groups.[106][105] At least 500,000 people were killed over the course of a few months, and hundreds of thousands others were detained.[c][110][111] The campaign destroyed the PKI and shifted power to the military.[112] The Supersemar order in 1966 gave Suharto de facto control over key executive and security powers, an effective transfer of power from Sukarno.[113][114]

Suharto's "New Order" restricted political organisation, embedded the military in government, and used his political party Golkar and a tightly controlled party system to dominate elections.[115] The Act of Free Choice in 1969 formally incorporated western New Guinea into Indonesia, but just over a thousand selected community leaders took part in it amid reports of military intimidation.[116] Many Papuans opposed this integration and have waged an armed resistance since then.[117][118] In 1975, Indonesia invaded Portuguese Timor and annexed the territory the following year.[119] Hasan di Tiro founded the Free Aceh Movement in 1976 and declared independence from Indonesia. The insurgency in Aceh was largely suppressed by 1979 but revived in 1989 after the return of fighters trained in Libya, prompting a military campaign lasting a decade.[120]

The New Order encouraged renewed foreign investment and sought foreign aid while pursuing industrialisation through state development plans.[121] From the 1970s, the regime greatly expanded the transmigration programme, resettling families from Java to other islands.[72] Manufacturing expanded and the number of people below the official poverty line fell substantially by the mid-1990s.[122] At the same time, conglomerates connected to Suharto's family and close associates accumulated wealth through state patronage and political protection.[123][124] The Asian financial crisis of 1997–98 caused a sharp economic downturn,[125][126] followed by protests and riots in May 1998, culminating in Suharto's resignation.[127] In a UN-supervised referendum in 1999, a majority of people in East Timor voted against remaining part of Indonesia.[128][d]

Reformasi and contemporary Indonesia

Main article: Reform era in Indonesia

The post-Suharto transition was marked by communal violence, including religious conflict in Maluku and ethnic clashes in Kalimantan.[130] This period, known as Reformasi, brought constitutional amendments, competitive elections, and decentralisation.[131][132] The military lost its reserved parliamentary seats, but their influence did not disappear.[133] Democratic institutions were established, but patronage and influence of oligarchy persisted.[134] Former general Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono won the first direct presidential election in 2004.[135] His administration reached a peace agreement with Aceh separatists in 2005 after the previous year's Indian Ocean tsunami brought more international attention to the province.[136] Sporadic bombings occurred throughout the 2000s but had declined by the early 2010s.[137]

Joko Widodo, popularly called Jokowi, was elected president in 2014 and prioritised infrastructure and economic development, which he linked to improving welfare.[138][139] Indonesia remained an electoral democracy, but the quality of its democracy declined amid weakened parliamentary opposition and oversight, curbs on dissent, reduced independence of the anti-corruption commission, and Jokowi's intervention in the 2024 election.[140][141] Under his successor Prabowo Subianto, the government pursued a fiscally expansive programme[142] and revised a military law in 2025, which allowed more active officers to serve in civilian posts.[143]

Geography

Main articles: Geography of Indonesia and List of islands of Indonesia

Indonesia is an equatorial archipelago of coastal plains, mountains, and volcanic islands. It lies between latitudes 11°S and 6°N and longitudes 95°E and 141°E,[146] and is the world's largest archipelagic state, extending 5,120 kilometres (3,181 mi) from east to west and 1,760 kilometres (1,094 mi) from north to south.[147] Several straits, including Malacca, Sunda, and Lombok, carry international traffic between the Indian and Pacific oceans, including ships transporting energy supplies and commercial cargo.[148][149]

The number of Indonesian islands varies by counting method, with published figures ranging from 13,466 named islands to more than 17,500.[150] About 922 of them are permanently inhabited.[151] Its five main islands are Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, Borneo, and New Guinea. Indonesia occupies most of Borneo, where it is known as Kalimantan, and the western part of New Guinea, commonly called Papua. The remainder of those islands is shared with Brunei and Malaysia, and with Papua New Guinea, respectively.[152]

Java accounts for less than 7% of Indonesia's land area but is its most populous island, with intensive farming and extensive urban growth.[153] Forest cover differs considerably, with larger forested areas in Papua and Maluku than in Java and Bali.[154] At 4,884 metres (16,024 ft), Puncak Jaya on New Guinea is the highest peak,[155] while Lake Toba on Sumatra is the largest lake.[156] In Kalimantan, major waterways like the Kapuas, Barito, and Mahakam rivers have historically served as corridors for movement and trade between communities in the interior and those near the coast.[157]

Indonesia occupies a complex plate-boundary zone where the Eurasian, India-Australia, and Pacific-Philippine sea tectonic plates interact, with subduction zones along these boundaries producing frequent earthquakes and volcanic activity.[158][159] The resulting volcanic belt contains roughly 400 volcanoes, of which around 130 are considered active.[160] This tectonic setting exposes the archipelago to major earthquake and tsunami hazards. The Sumatra earthquake in 2004 generated a tsunami that caused widespread destruction in Aceh.[161] The Toba super-eruption about 74,000 years ago is one of the largest known explosive eruptions in Earth's history,[162] and the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora was followed by global cooling and the Year Without a Summer in 1816.[163]

Climate

Main articles: Climate of Indonesia and Climate change in Indonesia

Indonesia's equatorial position and monsoon winds give it a tropical climate. Most lowland areas are warm and humid throughout the year, while higher terrain is cooler, and seasonal temperature differences are small.[164] Seasonal changes in the monsoon generally bring wetter conditions from November to April and drier conditions from May to October, but their timing and intensity vary by region.[164][165] Much of the country has a tropical rainforest climate, and tropical monsoon and savanna climates occur on parts of the islands.[166] Seasonal rainfall helps set rice-planting calendars and influences droughts, floods, and fires.[167][168][169]

Western Sumatra, western Java, and portions of Kalimantan and Papua receive the highest annual rainfall, whereas regions in closer proximity to Australia, such as Nusa Tenggara, experience a much drier climate.[170] The surrounding oceans, island geography, monsoon winds, and topography all affect where and when rain falls.[171] In drought-prone regions of the country, El Niño can suppress rainfall and prolong dry periods, causing water shortages and crop losses.[172][173]

Indonesia already faces climate-related hazards. Climate projections indicate further warming and sea-level rise, changes in rainfall patterns, and greater risks from extreme heat and flooding.[174][175] These changes affect agriculture, water resources, public health, coastal settlements and wildfire management.[176][177] Sea-level rise is especially relevant to coastal areas, where much of the population and infrastructure are located.[178][179] Evidence from Pekalongan in Central Java suggests that households with fewer economic resources and communities with weaker infrastructure may have less capacity to adapt.[180] The country is among the largest emitters of greenhouse gas emissions.[181]

Biodiversity and conservation

Main articles: Fauna of Indonesia, Flora of Indonesia, Environment of Indonesia, and Conservation in Indonesia
See also: List of biosphere reserves of Indonesia and List of national parks of Indonesia

Indonesia is among the 17 countries identified as megadiverse by Conservation International. Its many islands and geological history have helped produce a diverse flora and fauna.[183][184] Wallacea is a transition zone between Asian and Australian fauna and one of the world's largest centres of endemism.[185] In 2015, an estimated 83% of Southeast Asia's old-growth forest was in Indonesia.[186] Mangrove forests, coral reefs and seagrass beds make up much of the coastal ecosystems.[187]

Large oil-palm and timber plantations were estimated to account for more than 40% of national deforestation between 2001 and 2016.[188] Conversion of forest land for farming, roads, and other development breaks up remaining habitat, which affects species populations, habitat quality, and biodiversity.[189] Peat-swamp forests are important carbon stores and habitat for threatened taxa but are vulnerable to logging, fire and land conversion.[190] At sea, coral diversity has been found to be lower on polluted or anchor-damaged reefs, while coral cover has declined sharply during prolonged periods of extreme ocean heat.[191][192]

Indonesia has designated 554 protected areas covering 27 million hectares, equivalent to 14% of its land area.[193] Assessments conducted in 2015, 2017 and 2019 found improvements in management scores but identified poaching, illegal logging, human settlements, tourism and non-timber cultivation as the main threats to protected areas.[193] Social forestry programmes seeks to recognise customary communities' rights to manage forestland, but bureaucratic barriers have hindered its implementation.[194]

Government and politics

Main article: Politics of Indonesia
See also: Government of Indonesia

Indonesia is a unitary republic with a presidential system under the 1945 Constitution.[195][196] The constitution's five principles of Pancasila are taught through civic education.[197][198] After the fall of the New Order in 1998, four constitutional amendments between 1999 and 2002 altered the political system by introducing direct presidential elections, establishing new state institutions, reducing the role of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), and giving regional autonomy a constitutional basis.[199] Indonesia remained a unitary state, while decentralisation transferred substantial powers to the provinces, districts, and cities.[200]

The president is head of state, head of government,[196] and commander-in-chief of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and may serve no more than two five-year terms.[201] The MPR consists of elected members of the House of Representatives (DPR) and the Regional Representative Council (DPD).[202] The MPR may amend the constitution, inaugurate the president and vice-president, and dismiss them under constitutional procedures.[203] The DPR makes laws with the president, approves the state budget, and oversees the government.[204] The DPD may propose, review, and advise on bills concerning regional government[196] but has less authority than the DPR.[205]

The legal system belongs primarily to the civil-law tradition, while also incorporating customary (adat) law and Islamic law, including in marriage and inheritance matters for Muslims.[206] Judicial power is exercised by the Supreme Court, the courts beneath it, and the Constitutional Court.[207] The Supreme Court acts as the final appellate court and reviews regulations below statutes.[206] The Constitutional Court reviews statutes for constitutionality and decides disputes over state-institution powers, political party dissolution, and election results.[208] It also has a role in presidential impeachment proceedings.[209] The Religious Courts hear marriage, divorce and inheritance cases, as well as certain economic disputes arising under Islamic law.[210] The Judicial Commission proposes candidates for Supreme Court justices and has responsibilities concerning judicial conduct.[208]

Parties and elections

Main articles: List of political parties in Indonesia and Elections in Indonesia
Prabowo Subianto

Since the return to competitive elections in 1999, Indonesia has had a fragmented multi-party system.[211] No party has won a majority in legislative elections,[212] and presidents have usually governed through broad coalitions that include many parties in the legislature and cabinet.[213][214]

Political parties are often distinguished by their orientation towards secular nationalism or political Islam,[e][215] but governing coalitions commonly include both.[216] Party politics often relies more on patronage and elite power-sharing than detailed policy programmes,[217] although the role of Islam in public life is a source of ideological difference.[218] Opposition parties have at times joined presidential power-sharing arrangements after elections.[219]

Indonesia held its first general election in 1955.[220] Since 2004, voters have directly elected the president, the DPR, and the DPD every five years.[221] Members of the DPR are elected through party-based contests,[222] while DPD candidates run as individuals to represent provincial constituencies.[223] National elections require large-scale logistics, because ballots and other materials must reach remote islands, mountainous areas and places with limited infrastructure.[224]

Administrative divisions

Main article: Subdivisions of Indonesia

Indonesia is a unitary state divided into provinces, regencies and cities, each with elected regional authorities regulated by law.[225] Provinces are headed by governors and have provincial legislatures. Regencies and cities are headed by regents and mayors and have local legislatures.[225] They are divided into districts, which are further subdivided into villages and urban villages. Villages exercise local self-government, whereas urban villages form part of the district administration.[226][227]

Regional autonomy after 1998 transferred substantial powers to subnational governments, including provinces.[228] Special arrangements apply to nine of them: Aceh may apply aspects of Islamic law,[229] the six provinces in Papua have special autonomy,[230] and Yogyakarta retains a hereditary sultanate.[231] Jakarta has autonomy as the national capital.[232] Since 2022, Nusantara in East Kalimantan has been planned as the future national capital.[233]

Foreign relations and military

Main articles: Foreign relations of Indonesia and Indonesian National Armed Forces

Indonesia follows an "independent and active" (bebas aktif) foreign policy, a doctrine formulated by Vice President Mohammad Hatta in 1948.[235][236] The policy has emphasised non-alignment and independent action, along with a preference for diplomacy over military means in pursuing regional objectives.[237][238] One early expression of this policy was the hosting of the Bandung Conference in 1955, the precursor of the Non-Aligned Movement.[239] As a middle power, Indonesia works through regional and multilateral institutions while preserving room to manoeuvre in its relations with major powers.[240]

As a founding member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Indonesia places the organisation at the centre of its regional diplomacy.[241][242] Indonesia has broad bilateral ties with Malaysia and Singapore, including cooperation in economic, defence, and cultural fields.[243][244] Relations with Australia are conducted through a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership covering several areas, including economic development and regional stability.[245] On China–United States competition, Indonesia has avoided alliances and taking sides, emphasised an ASEAN-led regional approach and sought to limit escalation.[246]

Indonesia has been a member of the United Nations since 1950,[247] apart from an absence in 1965–66.[248][249] It participates in multilateral forums including the Non-Aligned Movement, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, and the East Asia Summit.[250] After decades as a major recipient of foreign aid,[251] Indonesia has been providing development assistance since 2015 and established a foreign aid agency in 2019.[252] Since 1957, it has sent military and police personnel to UN peacekeeping missions.[253]

The Indonesian National Armed Forces comprise the Army, Navy, and Air Force.[254] The Army's territorial units extend across provincial and regency/city areas.[255] Until its termination in 2000, the military's "dual function" (dwifungsi) doctrine provided a basis for involvement in political affairs alongside its security role.[256] By 2004, reforms had ended unelected military representation in Parliament and removed the military faction from the MPR.[257] Cooperative parliamentary oversight has helped stabilise civil–military relations, but has also hindered further reform and weakened democratic oversight of defence.[258]

Law enforcement and human rights

Main article: Human rights in Indonesia

Law enforcement is carried out by the Indonesian National Police, whose duties include maintaining public security and order, enforcing the law, and providing protection and services to the public.[260] The Chief of the Indonesian National Police is directly responsible to the president.[261]

The National Commission on Human Rights (Komnas HAM) is authorised to investigate human rights violations.[262] Accountability for past abuses has been limited. In 2024, the United Nations Human Rights Committee noted that only 4 of 16 violations investigated by Komnas HAM had reached the courts.[263] Indonesia practices the death penalty but has not executed anyone since 2016.[264]

Anti-Chinese racism has persisted despite the removal of most discriminatory policies after the New Order.[265] Since 2016, anti-LGBTQ campaigns have included hostile statements by public officials, police raids and proposals for criminal restrictions.[266] Religious minorities have also been affected by the country's blasphemy law.[267] In Papua, human rights monitors have reported extrajudicial killings and disappearances, restrictions on peaceful expression, and displacement due to security operations and armed conflict.[268]

Economy

Main articles: Economy of Indonesia, Agriculture in Indonesia, and Poverty in Indonesia

Indonesia has a mixed economy in which both the private sector and the government play major roles.[269][270] It is the only G20 member state in Southeast Asia.[271] In 2025, gross domestic product was Rp23.821 quadrillion (US$1.45 trillion) at current prices,[272][273] making it Southeast Asia's largest economy and placing it among the world's top 20 by nominal GDP and top 10 by GDP at purchasing power parity.[274] Services and industry account for the largest shares of gross domestic product,[275] while agriculture is the biggest source of employment.[276] The country's currency is the rupiah.[277]

The economy was once largely agricultural, and early post-independence policy focused on agricultural self-sufficiency. Industrial and urban growth increased from the late 1960s, speeding up in the 1980s as lower oil prices encouraged manufactured exports.[278] From the mid-1980s to the mid-1990s, trade barriers fell and export-oriented manufacturing expanded as economic growth continued and poverty declined.[279][280] The Asian financial crisis of 1997–98 caused a severe contraction and exposed weaknesses in the banking system.[281] Reforms during the recovery strengthened banking oversight, fiscal management and the exchange-rate regime. This helped the economy withstand later financial shocks, including the global financial crisis in 2008.[282] Following the COVID-19 pandemic, exports and public and private consumption helped restore economic growth.[283]

MSMEs generate more than 60% of national GDP and account for more than 90% of total employment.[284] Private consumption is also a major driver of growth.[285] Informal employment is widespread, including in agriculture, retail, and transport services.[286] Informal firms tend to have lower productivity and pay, and workers outside larger firms have more limited access to social insurance.[287] Businesses also have to contend with corruption, burdensome and sometimes conflicting local regulations, in addition to unreliable infrastructure such as power outages and congested roads.[288] Women's labour force participation has remained lower than men's since the 1990s.[289]

The official poverty rate was about 8% in March 2026.[290] Expenditure inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, stood at 0.368 in the same month and was higher in urban than in rural areas.[9] The social protection system generally places emphasis on supporting low-income populations. Mechanisms include conditional cash transfers and food assistance.[291]

Economic geography and sectors

Main articles: Tourism in Indonesia and Aquaculture in Indonesia
See also: Science and technology in Indonesia

The country's many islands affect where economic activity takes place and how goods move across the country.[293] Economic activity is concentrated on Java,[294] with Jakarta in particular accounting for a disproportionate share of national output.[295] Meanwhile, much of eastern Indonesia has weaker infrastructure and economies more dependent on agriculture.[294] High domestic transport costs hinder production and investment outside Java and make it harder to connect producers in the outer islands with major markets.[293][296]

The fisheries and aquaculture industry employs millions of people, particularly in coastal communities, and accounted for an estimated 2.5% of GDP in 2025.[297][298] Marine capture fisheries supply tuna and other seafood, while aquaculture produces shrimp, fish and seaweed. Exports of fisheries products reached US$6.27 billion in 2025, led by shrimp and tuna.[298][299] Indonesia is among the largest producers of marine capture fisheries, accounting for about 9% of global output in 2024.[300]

Tourism is a major service industry, contributing 4.5% to national GDP in 2024. It employs millions in businesses such as accommodation, food services, transport, and tourism goods retail.[301] The country's digital economy is the largest in Southeast Asia, reaching US$90 billion in gross merchandise value. E-commerce is the dominant sector,[302] and digital services have widened opportunities for small businesses.[284] However, access to them is uneven.[303]

Natural resource industries affect both investment and economic growth, which can rise or fall with commodity prices.[304] Policies since 2020 have encouraged more processing of commodities at home, particularly nickel.[305] Major exports include palm oil, coal, ferronickel and liquefied natural gas. Most export destinations are in Asia, but the United States and the European Union are also major markets.[306] Indonesia participates in regional economic cooperation through ASEAN and APEC and maintains trade and investment ties with the wider global economy, but its level of trade openness is relatively low compared with other ASEAN economies.[307]

Infrastructure

Main articles: Transport in Indonesia and Energy in Indonesia
See also: Communications in Indonesia

Infrastructure connects Indonesia's dispersed islands and supports trade, access to services and economic activity. The archipelagic geography has made infrastructure development costly and complicated, particularly in transport and logistics.[308] Telecommunications connectivity has expanded through the Palapa Ring fibre-optic network, although some remote areas are underserved.[309]

Shipping and domestic air services connect islands, including remote and outermost regions.[310] Road transport dominates passenger and freight movement, and reliance on personal vehicles regularly causes traffic congestion in cities where public transport is limited.[311] Rail transport is concentrated on Java, but new lines have recently begun operating in Sulawesi.[310] The Jakarta–Bandung high-speed railway, operating since 2023, is the first high-speed railway in the region.[312]

Indonesia produced nearly twice as much primary energy as it consumed in 2023, with coal dominating both primary energy production and electricity generation.[313] The state-owned electricity company Perusahaan Listrik Negara (PLN) controls transmission and distribution networks and purchases electricity from independent power producers for supply to the national grids.[314] Access to electricity is almost universal, but some remote communities remain out of reach of grids.[315][316] Indonesia ranked first globally in geothermal generation, although renewables supplied only a small share of electricity in 2023.[317]

Demographics

Main articles: Demographics of Indonesia and Indonesians
See also: List of Indonesian cities by population and List of metropolitan areas in Indonesia

The 2020 census recorded 270.2 million people,[7] making it the world's fourth most populous country after India, China and the United States.[318] The population is concentrated on Java and in urban centres, whereas many provinces outside Java and Bali are much less densely populated.[319][f] Java is home to 56.1% of the population,[321] and its population density is far above the national average,[g] reaching 1,171 people per square kilometre (3,030 people/mi2).[322]

Median age was 30.7 years in 2026,[323] while about 69% of the population was aged 15–64 in 2025.[324] An intercensal population survey in the same year shows that the total fertility rate has approached the replacement level, at 2.13 births per woman. Meanwhile, close to 12% of the population was aged 60 or older.[325]

Approximately 59% of Indonesians lived in urban areas as of 2025.[326] About 69% of urban households in the same year had access to adequate housing, based on national standards for living space, construction durability, drinking water and sanitation.[327] Jakarta is listed by the United Nations as the world's most populous city, with nearly 42 million inhabitants as of 2025.[h][330] Urbanisation has come from rural-to-urban migration, natural increase in urban areas, and the reclassification of rural settlements.[331] It has also expanded metropolitan regions, especially on Java,[332] and increased demand for infrastructure, basic services, and city management.[333]

An estimated 8 million Indonesians reside abroad, with large communities in Malaysia, the Netherlands, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and Taiwan. A large part of that population work in domestic service and other low-skilled jobs.[334]

Ethnic groups and languages

Main articles: Ethnic groups in Indonesia, Native Indonesians, and Languages of Indonesia

The 2010 census listed over 1,300 suku bangsa, or ethnic groups.[335] A later study in 2015 reclassified them into about 600 groups after noting classification difficulties.[336] Austronesian-speaking populations predominate in much of western and central Indonesia.[337] Melanesian populations live mainly in the eastern islands, including parts of Nusa Tenggara, Maluku, and Papua.[337][338] The Javanese are the largest ethnic group, making up about 40% of the population.[339] Other major groups include the Sundanese, Malay, Batak, Madurese, Betawi, Minangkabau, and Bugis.[340][i]

The official language, Indonesian, is a standardised variety of Malay based on the Riau-Johor literary tradition.[344] Malay had long served as a lingua franca in the archipelago before Indonesian nationalists adopted it as a language of unity through the 1928 Youth Pledge.[345] It gained official and formal status in 1945 under the name Bahasa Indonesia.[346] Written in the Latin script,[347] Indonesian has spread through education, government, and mass media, and serves as a common language across ethnic and regional boundaries.[348]

More than 700 languages are spoken across the archipelago.[349] These belong to two main language groups, Austronesian and Papuan.[350] Javanese is the most widely spoken local language and has official regional status in Yogyakarta.[351][352] Several regional languages have their own traditional writing systems, some of which are now used only to a limited extent.[353][354] Local languages remain part of regional identity and cultural heritage, even as Indonesian dominates national public life.[355] Dutch never became widely spoken as Malay was already the archipelago's lingua franca.[356] However, it remains important in some legal contexts.[357]

Religion

Main article: Religion in Indonesia

Indonesia recognises six religions: Islam, Protestantism, Roman Catholicism, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Confucianism,[360] while the constitution guarantees freedom of religion.[254] The state regulates religious affiliation and public worship. Recognised religions receive administrative recognition in matters of religious affiliation, marriages, and places of worship, but followers of indigenous religions often receive weaker recognition or face discrimination.[361] Pancasila makes belief in one God one of the state ideology's five principles and is used to support national unity and religious harmony.[362] Religious minorities still face discrimination, including through local religious bylaws, social pressure, and restrictions on worship.[363][364]

Indonesia has the largest Muslim population in the world,[365] with 251 million Muslims in 2025, or 87.15% of the population.[3][j] Christians make up 10.44% of the population and form majorities in several eastern provinces.[3][368] Hindus account for 1.66% and are concentrated in Bali,[3][359] while Buddhists account for 0.69% and are found mainly among Chinese Indonesians, though not exclusively.[3][369]

Many local belief systems predate major world religions and continue alongside them.[370][371] They include beliefs in ancestors, spirits, and powers associated with nature.[372][373] Traditions such as Sunda Wiwitan, Kejawèn, and Kaharingan continue in different forms within or alongside the recognised religions.[374][375][376] In Java and Bali, Islam and Hinduism also absorbed older customs and ritual practices.[377][378]

Education

Main article: Education in Indonesia

Indonesia's education system includes more than 50 million students and over 250,000 schools.[379] It is administered by ministries responsible for school education, higher education and religious education,[k] and follows a 6-3-3-4 structure: six years of elementary school, three years each of junior and senior secondary school, and four years of tertiary education.[380]

Since independence, schools have supported national integration through Indonesian-language instruction, national curricula, and civic education.[381] Access to education and school quality vary, particularly between urban and rural areas and among regions with differing levels of development.[382][383] Teacher quality and distribution are also persistent issues.[384] Student learning outcomes are low by OECD benchmarks. In PISA 2022, Indonesian 15-year-olds performed below OECD averages in mathematics, reading and science, with most not reaching the minimum proficiency level in each subject.[385]

Government expenditure on education was approximately 2.4% of GDP in 2024.[386] In 2022, Indonesia had 4,481 higher education institutions, including universities, Islamic institutions, service colleges, and open universities.[387] The University of Indonesia, Gadjah Mada University, and the Bandung Institute of Technology are among the highest-ranked public universities in international rankings.[388] Higher education has expanded since 1990 and contributes to better employment, but access, participation, and institutional quality are uneven.[389][390]

Healthcare

Main article: Healthcare in Indonesia

Primary care is provided mainly through community health centres (puskesmas) and primary-care hospitals.[391] In 2014, Indonesia launched Jaminan Kesehatan Nasional, one of the world's largest single-payer health-insurance systems that covered 98% of the population by 2024. Despite near-universal coverage, access to care and healthcare personnel still varies by location.[392] Government expenditure on healthcare was approximately 1.4% of GDP in 2024.[386]

Life expectancy increased between 1990 and 2019 from 62.5 to 69.4 years for men and from 65.7 to 73.5 years for women, but there are substantial differences between provinces.[393] Indonesia faces a double burden of disease. Non-communicable conditions have become increasingly prominent in overall health loss, and infectious diseases continue to contribute substantially to disability and premature mortality.[394] Stunting prevalence among children was 21.6% in 2022.[395]

Culture

Main article: Culture of Indonesia
See also: National Intangible Cultural Heritage of Indonesia

Cultures in Indonesia differ across islands, languages, and communities. Older populations and later Austronesian migrations contributed to this diversity, with Papuan and Melanesian populations prominent in the east.[396][397] Movement by sea placed the archipelago within trading and migration networks involving Indian, Arab, Persian, Chinese, and mainland Southeast Asian peoples, followed later by Europeans. Religious and courtly influences entered through these routes, and European expansion ultimately brought colonial domination. Coastal commercial centres often encountered outside influences before they reached inland communities.[398][399]

Indonesia has no single, uniform cultural tradition. Regional traditions are tied to particular languages and local cultures, while pan-Indonesian forms generally use Indonesian and are intended for audiences across regional and ethnic boundaries.[400][401] These traditions include performance, visual art, ritual, clothing, food, and literature.[402] Modern popular culture includes cinema, television drama, music, celebrity media and reality shows, along with imported Asian dramas and global formats adapted for Indonesian audiences.[403][404]

Indonesia has 16 items on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists, including wayang puppet theatre, batik, angklung, the saman dance, and pencak silat. Since 2024, joint nominations have added pantun, kebaya, and kolintang to the list.[405]

National identity and observances

Main articles: National symbols of Indonesia and Public holidays in Indonesia

Indonesia's national symbols include the red-and-white flag, the Garuda Pancasila emblem and the national anthem, Indonesia Raya.[406] The scroll on the Garuda emblem carries an Old Javanese motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, usually translated as "Unity in Diversity".[407] The phrase comes from Sutasoma, a 14th-century poem by Mpu Tantular that addressed relations between Buddhists and Hindus in Majapahit society. In its modern national usage, it expresses the ideal of unity among Indonesia's different ethnic, linguistic and religious communities.[408][409]

Pancasila, the country's foundational philosophy, comprises five principles, belief in one God, just and civilised humanity, national unity, democracy through deliberation and representation, and social justice. They appear in the preamble to the 1945 Constitution and have formed part of official efforts to define Indonesian national identity.[197][410] Other prominent social concepts include gotong royong (mutual assistance) and musyawarah (deliberation and consensus).[411] Adat encompasses customary norms and traditions that vary among communities.[412]

National holidays include Independence Day on 17 August and religious observances such as Eid al-Fitr, Christmas, Nyepi, Vesak and Chinese New Year.[413] Independence Day is commemorated through flag-raising ceremonies, community celebrations, and traditional competitions.[414] Eid al-Fitr, which follows Ramadan and locally called Lebaran, is associated with homecoming called mudik, family visits and gatherings seeking forgiveness.[415] In Bali, Nyepi is observed with a day of silence and restrictions on work and travel.[416]

Visual arts and architecture

Main articles: Indonesian art, Architecture of Indonesia, National costume of Indonesia, and Indonesian painting

Indonesian arts include textiles, puppetry, masks, carving, and painting.[417] Textiles are used in rituals and can convey social standing and ethnic affiliation. Colonial rule and nationalism affected the development of modern painting, and tourism and urban art communities became increasingly important later in the 20th century.[418] Regional painting traditions include Bali's classical Kamasan tradition, a narrative form often described as wayang painting.[419] Sculptural traditions range from megalithic monuments[29] to Ngaju Dayak hampatong figures and Asmat artefacts, serving commemorative, protective, aesthetic, or spiritual functions.[420][421]

Indonesian architecture ranges from everyday houses to ritual houses (rumah adat), whose layouts, posts, roofs, heirlooms, and construction rites can express ancestry, status, and local beliefs.[422] Regional forms include the Javanese pendapa, Dayak longhouses, Minangkabau Rumah Gadang, and Toraja Tongkonan.[423] Monumental religious architecture includes Borobudur and Prambanan,[424][425] while surviving Hindu and Buddhist sculpture from the 8th to 15th centuries includes works in stone, bronze, and gold.[426]

Clothing traditions differ by region and are used in ceremonies, weddings, formal occasions, and as markers of local identity.[427] Batik and kebaya are widely used in national and formal dress and are especially prominent in Javanese culture.[428] Other regional textile traditions include Minangkabau gold-thread textiles and distinctive ikat traditions among Batak and many eastern Indonesian communities. These textiles are used at formal events, in bridal exchanges and during ceremonies and weddings.[429]

Performing arts

Main articles: Music of Indonesia, Dance in Indonesia, and Theatre of Indonesia

Indonesian music and dance include court, village, ritual, and popular forms. Gamelan traditions are centred especially in Java and Bali, while angklung and other bamboo ensembles are used in western Java, Banyumas, and other regions. Drums, gongs, lutes and singing often accompany dance.[430] Islamic musical forms include gambus and qasida,[431] while popular genres include keroncong and dangdut.[432] The latter developed from Melayu music and draws on Indian, Arabic and Western pop and rock influences.[433]

Mask dances appear in Javanese court drama and Balinese ritual performance, while Dayak mask dances are performed in agricultural rituals and communal ceremonial settings.[434] Javanese court dance includes forms such as bedhaya and serimpi, while other local dances are associated with theatre and music, spirit possession, harvests, temple festivals, cremation ceremonies, and commemorations of the dead.[435] Contemporary performers also adapt global forms.[436][437]

Traditional Indonesian theatre encompasses storytelling, music, movement, puppetry, masks, acting, and dance.[438] Wayang is a prominent puppet-theatre tradition in Java that is also practised in Bali. Led by a dalang and accompanied by gamelan music, its repertory frequently reworks episodes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.[439][440] It has served ritual, moral, comic, political, and public-messaging functions.[441][442] Other regional traditions combine drama with music, dance, masks, or martial arts,[443] and modern theatre groups have used their performances for social and political commentary.[444][445]

Literature

Main article: Indonesian literature

Literary traditions developed in many regional languages and included both oral and written forms.[446][447] Oral traditions ranged from storytelling to songs, customs, beliefs, and other community forms, and material could move between oral and written forms.[448] Traditional written literature includes court chronicles, religious and legal writing, narrative prose, and verse. These forms often served ethical, religious, or dynastic purposes rather than entertainment.[449]

Modern literature grew in the early 20th century alongside the expansion of literacy, publishing, and a wider reading public.[450] Balai Pustaka, established in 1917, distributed books and maintained libraries and agencies across the archipelago, which gave writers access to wider circulation.[451] During this period, prose fiction and poetry became more prominent, displacing some older literary forms.[452] From 1933, Pujangga Baru provided another venue for literary and cultural writing, publishing essays, poetry, short stories, and longer prose before the Japanese occupation.[453] Newspapers, magazines, and other publications carried Indonesian-language prose and poetry during the prewar period.[454]

In the 1970s and 1980s, newspapers and magazines were important outlets, with regular sections carrying poetry, short stories, criticism, and serial fiction.[455] From the late 1990s, some forms of literary activity began to emerge in digital media, as websites, mailing lists, forums and blogs provided spaces for literary communities and publication.[456] Post-1998 literary production has faced fewer state restrictions,[457] allowing writers to address previously sensitive subjects, including sexuality and stronger religious expression, more openly.[458]

Cinema and mass media

Main articles: Cinema of Indonesia and Mass media in Indonesia

Indonesian film production began during the Dutch colonial era with Loetoeng Kasaroeng (1926), and a small number of film companies emerged after independence.[461] Film became a vehicle for nationalist and anti-imperialist politics under Sukarno,[462] while the New Order regulated and censored cinema.[463] The domestic industry of the 1970s and 1980s declined sharply in the early 1990s.[464] After 1998, independent filmmakers, film communities, festivals, and renewed commercial production helped revive Indonesian cinema.[465][466] However, censorship and pressure from non-state actors still limited expression.[467]

During the New Order, newspapers and broadcasters operated under licensing and censorship,[468] and television was used to advance state-led development and a unified vision of national identity.[469] In the Reformasi period, the 1999 Press Law ended government censorship and publication bans, and removed the requirement for publishing licences, but journalists and news organisations continued to face lawsuits, intimidation and physical attacks, sometimes involving government officials.[470]

Internet use grew rapidly from the mid-1990s, and websites provided another means of distributing news and information.[471][472] Mainstream news organisations increasingly use the same reporting across television, print and online outlets, either through integrated newsrooms or by sharing content between them. News is also shortened or reformatted for websites and social media.[473]

Cuisine

Main article: Indonesian cuisine

Indonesian cuisine differs from one region to another in its ingredients, methods, and flavours. Trade and migration brought Indian, Chinese and Middle Eastern influences over centuries, and Portuguese and other European traders arriving from the 16th century, followed by Dutch colonial rule, introduced further ingredients and cooking practices.[474][475] Indonesian cuisine also spread abroad, particularly to the Netherlands, where cookbooks and migration introduced Indonesian food to Dutch society by the late 19th century.[476]

Rice is the staple food in much of the country and is commonly served with meat or fish, vegetables, sambal, and other condiments.[477] Chilli, coconut milk, shrimp paste, peanuts, garlic, shallots, and tamarind are widely used in cooking, along with foods such as chicken and seafood.[478] Peanuts are used to make sauces for dishes such as gado-gado and sate.[479]

Tempeh and tahu (tofu) are widely consumed soybean products. Tempeh originated in Java and is also eaten in Bali and elsewhere in Indonesia.[479] Mie (noodles) and nasi goreng are also popular dishes.[480] Regional cuisines include Minangkabau dishes such as rendang.[479] Tumpeng is a Javanese ceremonial rice dish served for life-cycle events and other communal observances, where it is associated with gratitude and blessing.[481]

Sports

Main article: Sports in Indonesia

Popular sports in Indonesia include football, badminton, weightlifting, and basketball, along with local games and martial arts.[482] Football is one of the most followed sports, with active club supporters and public screenings of matches.[483] The national football team was the first Asian representative to appear at the FIFA World Cup, taking part in the 1938 tournament as the Dutch East Indies.[484]

Indonesia has been particularly successful in international badminton, winning both the Thomas and Uber Cups, the men's and women's world team championships.[485] Most of Indonesia's Olympic medals have come from badminton and weightlifting.[486] Indonesia first competed at the Olympics in 1952 and has participated in the Asian Games since their inaugural edition in 1951. Jakarta has hosted the Asian Games twice, first in 1962 and again in 2018 with Palembang.[487]

Traditional sports and games are featured in ceremonies, harvest events, contests, and public entertainment. Examples include sepak takraw, bull racing (karapan sapi) in Madura,[488] and ritual combat traditions such as caci in Flores and pasola in Sumba.[489] Pencak silat is a form of Indonesian martial arts and was included as an official event at the 2018 Asian Games, where Indonesia won all 14 gold medals contested in the sport.[490][491]
